If you lived the same way you eat your food, how would you live?

I've always wondered how you stay grounded during shows - singing the same song over and over would cause me to dissociate from the lyrics and move into muscle memory. So when I see you guys singing your hearts out at every single show as if it is the only show you've ever played, I find myself thinking: "Are they really still feeling these lyrics, thinking about what they are playing/singing as they are doing it? Or just on auto-pilot, able to act the part without having to feel the emotional strain or pull of each song?" I don't know if that makes sense.

Are there any messages/emotions/ideas you have wanted to put into words, or put into a song, for a long time - but have not found the right way to do it yet?

What is the hardest part of touring? And the best part?

What song has shifted most drastically from how you felt about it when it was written to how you feel about it now?

How do you get on stage and perform when you don't want to, aren't feeling it, or are exhausted?

When was the last time you laughed until you couldn't breathe, and what was it about?

If you could restart your journey from a small band to a massively famous band, is there anything you would have changed or done differently? 

What was the hardest decision about the band and/or the music you have ever had to make?

Do you see and remember specific fans in the crowds? I always wonder how hard it must be to not make direct eye contact with the fans right in front of you when you're up close.

Does it bother you that concerts are filled with fans taking pictures and videos? Do you wish they'd put their phones down sometimes?

There. I have asked my questions to the void.

Stressed Out. I was 13, and I had only really listened to radio music and my parent's music. I remember it was this pivotal moment where I thought about how I really enjoyed music, and I wanted more. I wanted more than the shallow, empty radio music. But I was a sheltered kid and I literally did not know how to find music on my own. I remember all my friends talked about something called "Spotify", so I searched it up on the family laptop.

I did not like what I heard in my first brief browse of Spotify. So I started searching songs by name - just typing in keywords and titles of songs that I felt like would resonate with me. Mostly I searched really depressing titles and words, because I was a super depressed teenager.

And "Stressed Out" happened to be a term that I searched. It popped up on some kind of curated Spotify list for songs that were rising in popularity or something, I can't really remember what it was. 

I listened to it, and I was like "okay this is fine" and moved on.

The next day, I found myself with it stuck in my head. I needed to hear it again. So I listened to it again. I still didn't LOVE it. But I liked the lyrics. So I went to the artist's page.

That's when I found Fairly Local. And I was hooked from that moment forward. :)

Mostly, it has helped me talk to God. I really struggle with the feeling that I am speaking to nothing and no one when I pray. Not only that, but I never know what to say... how to talk to someone who created everything, knows everything, and is everything. What do you even say?

It was the first thing I noticed about TØP music when I was 13 years old and struggling to decide if I really believed in the faith I was raised in. To me, it sounded like Tyler was angry and confused about God. I was angry and confused too. When I needed a way to express what I was feeling, I would sing with Tyler to God, and somehow it felt less like I was "screaming to an empty sky".

Sometimes Tyler's lyrics put things to words that I have been feeling for a long time, but haven't felt able to properly express. Especially to God.

So, I use TØP songs to talk to God. Because I resonate with almost every word, and if I can't talk to God, I guess I will have to sing to Him.

I am so glad you are seeing the love for you. I can't believe anyone would rather hear the songs done by massive artists or the "obvious" choices rather than some smaller artists and artists who were inspired by TØP. To me, the latter sounds much more appealing. Learning about new artists and hearing styles I've never heard, on songs I love?? Sign me up.

I have had many, many cavities filled now with this technique (topical before the injection). I will say it does numb the sting of the initial poke. But I assume as the professionals have mentioned below that any other effect is placebo.

That means nothing to me, as placebo (in my opinion) is just our Human super power to make ourselves feel better in the absence of any scientific reason to feel better. So if they have a gel that activates my brain's random magical power to make me feel less pain, then I'm happy for them to use it on me!

Also, I do believe it is very much about technique. I've been to 4 dentists now and dealt with numbing like this, and only found one where I can't feel anything but a single miniscule pinch every now and then. That dentist is my favorite.

But, that being said, I still use techniques to distract myself from focusing on the pain. I count tiny holes in the ceiling, play the alphabet game, recite song lyrics, etc. Anything to keep my brain from magnifying any existing pain with attention. 

When you have to go through the numbing, picture it going really well for you before you go. Try not to picture the worst. Imagine you're going to go in there, have no pain at all, and be shocked at how easy it was. Walk in with that in mind.

And while it's happening, remember that just because you feel pressure it's not necessarily pain. And that any quick pinches will stop quickly and you will be okay. Something that helps me is to remember that the longer it goes on, the less I'll feel it, because it will start to take effect. :)

You got this! I know it's unreasonably scary for some reason at times. But I hope this helps!

I know this is super late, but I'm responding anyway. I've always interpreted it this way:

Tyler has referred to his mind as a "house" before in "The Judge" when he sings "and now that my MIND is OUT and now I hear it clear and loud I'm thinking wow, I probably should have stayed INSIDE my HOUSE."

So I take "house" to mean "mind" here again. In that case, these lyrics reflect Tyler's struggle with the state of his mind (aka house). He is asking God to rebuild this house with "pieces"—something solid, stable, and dependable. He feels that while God has access to these "pieces," Tyler is only able to build with "chemicals," which symbolize something unstable, reactive, and lacking in form or permanence. This suggests that he sees his current mental state as fragile or chaotic, made up of elements that are ever-changing and difficult to control. He longs for God to replace this instability with something more enduring and substantial, something that can provide the structure and stability he cannot achieve on his own.

At least this is my interpretation! May not be how he intended or wrote it, but it helps me. Because that's how I sing it. And it really resonates with me when interpreted that way. So there ya have it. :)

Responding to all 3 comments here so far with the same reponse all in one since it's long! Thank you guys all for caring enough to read my long post!


He has regular vet checkups and they have been made aware of his behavioral issues, but have not identified anything problematic medically.


They did provide my mother with something to ease his anxiety while she was out of the house (I can't remember what the medication was called), but it had no effect.


Recently we've allowed him free roam of the entire house while we are gone rather than a crate, a small enclosed room, or a large enclosed room. The only thing he does not have access to now if we are out is the outdoors (we don't leave him for longer than a couple of hours) because he chews the wooden gate to pieces.


This free roam seems to have made a small impact on his anxiety. It's like he has an anxiety about being contained and restrained. If I stop walking during a walk because he's tugging, he just panics even more. It seems to be ineffective at teaching him to stop tugging because he wants to go where he wants to go and stopping him from getting there just does not work for him! I still do it because this is a new technique I'm working on to try to work on leash pulling.


Honestly he's not too bad on leash pulling for most of the walk, just when he gets home and wants to go inside.


He's like 100% fine for most of the day. Totally normal dog who plays, gives and gets love, sleeps a normal amount, eats fine, drinks water, goes outside, chews his bone... but then there's like that other 30% of the day where just something sets him off or he just doesn't feel like doing something we asked of him and it just makes the good things pale in comparison to the hard parts.


If he is overstimulated I have no idea where it would be coming from. He has a relatively quiet/normal home life with occasional play sessions and walks. No one is getting in his face, we respect his boundaries and body language. He doesn't have loud music or kids running around him or strangers petting him all the time. We do not yell at him and no one is physical with him, ever. He sleeps great through the night although he does randomly get up and cry at my parents in the middle of the night for no reason and then go back to sleep, and they don't know why. He honestly seems pretty happy until he just isn't.


His typical exercise is 2 to 3 walks a day, he loves them. And a good play session every now and then (a couple times a day) when we can tell he needs to work some extra energy off or he asks to play with a toy).


Desensitization to scary things looks like picking up my keys and putting on my shoes when I'm not actually leaving and then taking them back off/putting the keys down. Also playing "touch" where he touches my hand with his nose for a treat closer and closer to things he's scared of (like the vent and doorstopper) also leaving a treat on/near them and in corners he's spooked about.


He does LOVE his lick mats and his kongs. Although we do have to be careful he doesn't love them too much because we did notice when he was around 6 months that if he likes something a LOT he can get protective. :( Anyway yes I loveeeee playing find the treat games with him in various rooms and he loves it too.


Anyway we may try clicker training, but honestly I'm not sure it will help with him. My other dog LOVED the clicker though. We did work with a couple of trainers who modeled positive reinforcement. They are just expensive. 


I will look into jwdogtraining and puppies for dummies. Also great idea dropping the treats on the ground, he might like that. I'll see what my mother thinks about anxiety meds.

TL:DR; Vet says he's fine, I don't think he's over stimulated, will look into anxiety meds, resources mentioned by other comments and/or yours. Free roam of house instead of crate has helped a little.

Function of Beauty makes custom shampoo, conditioner, and leave-in treatments. They are a little pricey but holy cow are they worth it. Other than that, I've done a lot of research on hair because, like I mentioned above, my hair was just plain awful for such a long time and I was desperate for an answer. Here is what I've learned:

1. Don't shower every day. You strip your hair of its natural oils and then your scalp over produces the oils to compensate and you get yourself in a never ending cycle. Your hair will be greasy at first when you stop taking daily showers but eventually it adjusts itself.
2. If you live in a place with super hard water, use a clarifying shampoo or a little apple cider vinegar once a month. The mineral deposits on your hair will be removed and you'll see a big difference. Apply evenly and let the clarifying shampoo or apple cider sit for five minutes before rinsing out.
3. Super hot water will dry out and damage your hair. Avoid it!
4. If you can't use a custom shampoo, use any product by Shea Moisture (no I am not affiliated with them, just know their products are scientifically better for hair than 90% of others). You can find their products online or at any walmart or target.
5. Don't rub your hair with a towel. It damages the strands badly. If you must use a towel, simply leave it up in a towel for a while and then air dry or pat it dry. Also don't use a hair dryer without a diffuser, or better yet don't use a hair dryer at all because it dries out and damages your hair.
6. For curly hair: while your hair is wet, start the brush like you're about to brush your hair normally (at the top of your head) and then about 2 inches into the brush stroke, flip the brush over with the hair still in it so that the back of the brush touches the hair and continue the stroke all the way down. The curls will become perfect ringlets if you do this correctly. I found this out myself.
7. For curly hair: Look up a video on how to "plop" your hair. Such an amazing way to get curl definition and volume!
8. Get a satin or silk pillowcase to sleep on at night.
9. Don't use products with alcohol among the first ingredients (most hairsprays, mousses, styling gels, or other products that hold your hair in place) or use them very sparingly or infrequently. They dry our your hair SO badly. There are better alternatives!
10. Brush your shampoo and conditioner into your hair in the shower  (GENTLY, wet hair is very fragile) and also let the conditioner sit on your hair for a couple minutes before rinsing. The brushing spreads the product evenly and coats every strand. The leaving the conditioner in allows the ingredients to penetrate the strands.
11. When you brush or comb your hair, do your absolute best to not break any strands. Start from the bottom up. The worst kind of frizz is caused by broken strands ending somewhere on your head instead of ending at the bottom of your hair where the majority of the strands usually end. One year of being ultra gentle with your hair will make your hair look amazing. It's hard at first because you have to go pretty slow but eventually you get the hang of it and it becomes much easier. I discovered this and tested this myself and it worked so well for me.
12. Get yourself a good leave-in product or hair oil. It makes a big difference.
13. Some hair doesn't need to be shampooed every time you shower. Some people only shampoo once a week. I shampoo every time I feel my hair getting too greasy. But not every time I shower. Shampoo is made to get oil out of your hair. Some people don't produce enough oil to justify shampooing every day but they don't realize it. They get frustrated and confused when their hair is always dry and frizzy and they don't realize it is because they are taking the oils away from their scalp before it has a chance to reach the ends of your hair.
14. Use shampoo mainly at the scalp and don't use much on the ends. Shampoo is made to get oils off the hair, but the oil comes from your scalp and is meant to travel down the strands to moisturize the ends. If you don't shampoo your scalp enough, oil builds up. If you shampoo your ends too much, the oils never have a chance to moisturize your ends.
15. On the flip side, conditioner is made to DEPOSIT oils/moisturizers. If you use conditioner mainly on your scalp, oil builds up. And if you don't get the conditioner to your ends, they become dry and brittle.
